q: The word 'SOCIALIST' was inserted into the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by which Amendment?

q: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution declares India to be a:
o: B. Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
e: The Preamble reads: 'We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic...'

q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be used to interpret its provisions?
o: B. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
C. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
D. Minerva Mills v. Union of India
e: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court by a 7:6 majority held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution. Earlier in Berubari Case (1960), the SC held the Preamble was not part of the Constitution. Concept note: Basic Structure Doctrine: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but CANNOT destroy its 'basic structure.' The Preamble reflects the basic structure. Key elements include: supremacy of Constitution, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, and judicial review.

q: The right to property was a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31. It was deleted and made a constitutional/legal right under Article 300-A by which Amendment?
e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, and inserted Article 300-A making the right to property only a legal right, not a Fundamental Right.

q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the Right to Equality before law and equal protection of law?
e: Article 14 provides that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

q: The doctrine of 'Reasonable Classification' under Article 14 requires:
o: A. The classification must be based on intelligible differentia only
B. The differentia must have a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved
e: Two cumulative tests under Article 14: (1) intelligible differentia — the basis of classification must be clear and distinct; (2) rational nexus — the classification must be rationally connected to the object of the law. Leading case: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952). Concept note: Article 14 prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification. Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously — intelligible differentia AND rational nexus to the object of the legislation.

q: 'Arbitrariness' as a ground to strike down state action under Article 14 was evolved in which case?
o: A. R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
B. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib
C. E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
D. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
e: In E.P. Royappa (1974), the Supreme Court held that equality is antithetic to arbitrariness and any arbitrary State action violates Article 14. This expanded Article 14 beyond mere 'reasonable classification' to strike down arbitrary executive action.

q: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of:
o: A. Religion, Race, Caste, Language, Place of birth
B. Religion, Race, Caste, Sex, Place of domicile
C. Religion, Race, Caste, Sex, Place of birth
D. Religion, Caste, Language, Sex, Place of birth
e: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination ONLY on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Language and domicile are NOT included in Article 15.

q: Which Article enables the State to make special provisions for women and children?
e: Article 15(3) provides that nothing in Article 15 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children. Article 15(4) is for backward classes.

q: The concept of 'substantive due process' under Indian Constitutional Law was evolved through the interpretation of which Article?
e: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the SC held that the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable — importing substantive due process into Indian Constitutional Law. Concept note: Article 21 Expansion: Originally in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), Article 21 was narrowly interpreted. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the SC held procedure must be just, fair and reasonable. Post-Maneka, Article 21 has been expanded to include right to livelihood, right to privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), right to health, right to education (now 21-A), right to dignified death, etc.

q: Right to Education as a Fundamental Right was inserted as Article 21-A by which Constitutional Amendment?
e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21-A providing free and compulsory education to children between 6–14 years as a Fundamental Right.

q: Which case held that 'Right to Privacy' is a Fundamental Right under Article 21?
o: A. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
B. Joseph Shine v. Union of India
C. NALSA v. Union of India
D. Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
e: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge constitutional bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution.

q: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the Right against exploitation — prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour?
e: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous work.

q: Freedom of religion is guaranteed under Articles:
e: Articles 25–28 deal with freedom of religion. Articles 29–30 deal with cultural and educational rights of minorities.

q: Which of the following Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a National Emergency declared under Article 352?
o: C. All Fundamental Rights except Articles 20 and 21
e: The 44th Amendment, 1978 made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even during a National Emergency. All other Fundamental Rights can be suspended by Presidential Order under Article 359.

q: Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
e: Part III contains Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35). Part IV contains Directive Principles (Articles 36–51). Part IVA contains Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A).

q: Directive Principles are NOT enforceable in court. Which Article makes this explicit?
e: Article 37 states that the provisions in Part IV shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country.

q: In the conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, which prevails according to Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)?
o: C. There is a harmonious balance; neither can destroy the other
D. Parliament can decide case by case
e: In Minerva Mills (1980), the Court struck down provisions of the 42nd Amendment which gave absolute primacy to DPSPs, holding that harmony between Parts III and IV is itself a basic feature of the Constitution. Concept note: FR vs DPSP Evolution: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — FRs prevailed; Golaknath (1967) — FRs unamendable; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — both can coexist; Minerva Mills (1980) — harmony between Parts III and IV is basic structure.

q: Which Directive Principle directs the State to organize village panchayats?
e: Article 40 directs the State to take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.

q: Fundamental Duties are contained in which Article of the Constitution?
e: Article 51-A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, contains the Fundamental Duties. The 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

q: How many Fundamental Duties are currently in Article 51-A?
e: Originally 10 Fundamental Duties were inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The 11th duty — to provide opportunities for education to children between 6-14 years — was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).

q: The 'golden triangle' in Constitutional Law refers to:
e: The 'golden triangle' of Articles 14, 19, and 21 was evolved in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978). Any law that affects these rights must pass the test of all three Articles.

q: Article 13 declares void any law that is inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights. The phrase 'law' here includes:
o: C. Laws in force including ordinances, regulations, customs and usages
e: Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage. Constitutional amendments were held NOT to be 'law' under Article 13 in Kesavananda Bharati.

q: Which Article gives the Supreme Court power to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
e: Article 32 is the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (Dr. Ambedkar). It gives the Supreme Court power to issue writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

q: Article 32 and Article 226 — what is the distinction?
o: A. Art. 32 is for SC; Art. 226 is for High Courts; Art. 226 is wider in scope
B. Art. 32 is for SC; Art. 226 is for High Courts; Art. 32 is wider
C. Art. 226 can only be used for Fundamental Rights enforcement
D. Both are identical in scope
e: Article 32 is for Supreme Court — only for Fundamental Rights enforcement. Article 226 is for High Courts — wider, can be used for enforcement of any legal right, not just Fundamental Rights.

q: The executive power of the Union is vested in:
e: Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President. However, the President is a constitutional head who acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74).

q: The President of India is elected by:
o: B. Elected members of Parliament only
C. Elected members of Parliament + Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
D. All members of Parliament + all members of State Legislatures
e: The electoral college consists of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members and members of State Legislative Councils are excluded.

q: Article 74(1) provides that the Council of Ministers headed by the PM shall 'aid and advise' the President. After the 44th Amendment, the President:
o: A. Can refer it back once but must act on revised advice
C. Must consult the Supreme Court before acting
D. Shall act in accordance with such advice
e: The 44th Amendment (1978) added a proviso to Article 74(1): The President may return the advice for reconsideration, but if re-tendered, the President shall act accordingly.

q: The Governor of a State is appointed by:
e: Article 155 provides that the Governor of each State shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

q: Which Article empowers the Parliament to legislate on State List subjects in the national interest?
e: Article 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on State List subjects if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3 majority declaring it is necessary or expedient in the national interest.

q: 'Colorable Legislation' refers to a situation where:
o: A. The legislature tries to do indirectly what it cannot do directly
B. Legislation is unconstitutional due to mala fide intent

q: The Union List, State List, and Concurrent List are contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
e: The Seventh Schedule contains three lists: List I (Union List — 97 entries), List II (State List — 66 entries), and List III (Concurrent List — 47 entries). Currently List I has 100 entries.

q: In case of repugnancy between a Union law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject, which prevails under Article 254?
o: C. The later law prevails regardless of maker
e: Under Article 254(1), if there is a repugnancy between Union and State laws on a Concurrent List subject, the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy. Exception under Article 254(2): if the State law has received Presidential assent, it prevails in that State.

q: Which Article provides for Inter-State Council for coordination between States and the Union?
e: Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if it appears to him that the public interests would be served by the establishment of such a council.

q: Article 200 deals with:
o: A. Money Bills in State Legislature
C. Assent to Bills by the President
D. Assent to Bills by the Governor
e: Article 200 provides that when a Bill has been passed by the State Legislature, it shall be presented to the Governor who shall declare his assent, withhold assent, return (non-money bill) for reconsideration, or reserve it for the President.

q: The concept of 'Implied Powers' in constitutional interpretation means:
o: A. Powers not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution
D. Powers that can be inferred from express provisions
e: Implied powers are those which are not expressly mentioned but are necessary to carry out the express powers. The doctrine is used to fill gaps in legislative competence.

q: Residuary powers under Article 248 vest in:
e: Article 248 gives Parliament exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent or State List (residuary powers). Entry 97 of List I also confirms residuary powers.

q: Independence of the judiciary is secured by which provision among others?
o: A. Salaries charged to Consolidated Fund of India
e: Judicial independence is secured through multiple mechanisms: fixed salaries charged to Consolidated Fund (not subject to vote), security of tenure until retirement age, removal only through impeachment process.

q: The process of appointment of Supreme Court judges — the 'Collegium System' — was evolved through:
o: A. All three together established the current system
e: First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta, 1981) — Executive primacy. Second Judges Case (1993) — Collegium system; CJI's opinion gets primacy. Third Judges Case (1998) — Collegium = CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges. NJAC (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in 2015. Concept note: Three Judges Cases: The current collegium system where the Chief Justice and 4 senior-most judges recommend appointments gives the judiciary primacy over executive in judicial appointments. The NJAC established by 99th Amendment (2014) was struck down as violative of judicial independence — itself a basic structure element.

q: Article 141 provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on:
o: C. All courts in India except the Supreme Court itself
e: Article 141 provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. The Supreme Court itself follows the principle of stare decisis but is not absolutely bound by its own decisions.

q: The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in disputes between States is provided under:
e: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between two or more States.

q: Article 136 — Special Leave Petition (SLP) — grants the Supreme Court:
e: Article 136 grants the Supreme Court wide discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order of any court or tribunal in India.

q: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) as a concept is an extension of:
o: C. Article 32 and Article 226 jurisdiction (epistolary jurisdiction)
e: PIL evolved through liberalization of locus standi under Articles 32 and 226. The SC allowed any public-spirited person to write a letter (epistolary jurisdiction) to approach the court on behalf of those unable to access justice. Pioneered by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer.

q: Which Article provides for the High Court's power of superintendence over all subordinate courts?
e: Article 227 gives every High Court the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.

q: The doctrine of 'judicial review' in India covers:
o: A. Constitutionality of legislative and executive action only
C. Legislative acts, executive actions, and constitutional amendments (subject to basic structure)
e: Judicial review in India covers three areas: (1) legislative acts — struck down if violate Constitution; (2) executive/administrative actions — struck down if ultra vires, unreasonable, or against natural justice; (3) constitutional amendments — struck down if they violate basic structure (post-Kesavananda Bharati).

q: Article 352 deals with which type of Emergency?
e: Article 352 deals with National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. Article 356 is President's Rule. Article 360 is Financial Emergency.

q: During a National Emergency, Article 358 suspends which rights automatically?
e: Article 358 provides for automatic suspension of Article 19 freedoms when a National Emergency is proclaimed on grounds of war or external aggression. Article 359 requires a Presidential Order for suspending other FRs (but NOT Articles 20 & 21).

q: National Emergency under Article 352 can be proclaimed by the President on the written advice of:
e: After the 44th Amendment (1978), the proclamation of National Emergency requires the written advice of the Cabinet (Council of Ministers). The Prime Minister alone cannot advise such proclamation — it must be a Cabinet decision in writing.

q: President's Rule under Article 356 can be imposed when:
o: A. The State government violates Fundamental Rights
B. The constitutional machinery of the State has failed
D. There is financial mismanagement in the State
e: Article 356 can be invoked when the President is satisfied on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. Concept note: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): 9-judge bench held Art. 356 is subject to judicial review. Floor of the House is the only place to test majority. Secularism is a basic feature — a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed under Art. 356.

q: The maximum period for which Financial Emergency under Article 360 can operate continuously without Parliament's approval:
o: A. Indefinitely with Parliament's approval every 2 months initially
e: Unlike National Emergency and President's Rule, Financial Emergency under Article 360 has NO maximum period. Once proclaimed and approved by Parliament, it continues until the President revokes it. Initial approval must be within 2 months.

q: For continuation of National Emergency after one month, approval must be by:
o: B. Both Houses separately by simple majority
C. Special majority of Parliament (2/3 of total membership + majority present and voting)
e: National Emergency requires approval by special majority: not less than two-thirds of the members of each House of Parliament present and voting AND a majority of the total membership of each House.

q: The 44th Amendment, 1978 made which key change regarding Emergency provisions?
o: B. Changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' and required Cabinet's written advice
e: The 44th Amendment (1978) made key changes: (1) substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance'; (2) required Cabinet's written advice before proclamation; (3) made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable; (4) raised the majority required for approval.

q: Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) was significant because:
o: B. It held that President's Rule proclamation under Article 356 was entirely non-justiciable
C. It first established the collegium system
D. It invalidated imposition of President's Rule
e: In Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977), the Supreme Court held that the proclamation under Article 356 was non-justiciable. This position was later overruled by the landmark S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

q: The special provisions for certain States are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
e: Part XXI of the Constitution (Articles 369-392) contains temporary, transitional and special provisions including special provisions for certain States under Articles 370-371J.

q: Article 370, which granted special status to Jammu & Kashmir, was:
o: A. Struck down by Supreme Court
C. Its operative provisions abrogated by Presidential Order in August 2019
e: Presidential Order CO 272 (2019) effectively abrogated Article 370's special provisions. J&K was reorganized into two Union Territories — J&K and Ladakh. The Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in Dr. Farooq Abdullah v. Union of India (2023).

q: Article 371 relates to special provisions for which State?
e: Article 371 — Maharashtra and Gujarat. Article 371-A — Nagaland. Article 371-B — Assam. Article 371-C — Manipur. Article 371-D — Andhra Pradesh. Article 371-F — Sikkim. Article 371-G — Mizoram. Article 371-H — Arunachal Pradesh.

q: Which Article allows Parliament to provide for the establishment of local legislatures or Councils of Ministers for Union Territories?
e: Article 239-A was inserted by the 14th Amendment, 1962. It allows Parliament to create a body to function as a Legislature or a Council of Ministers or both for certain Union Territories.

q: The Election Commission of India is established under which Article of the Constitution?
e: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament and State Legislatures in the Election Commission of India.

q: The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office:
o: A. Only in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge
B. By a resolution of Parliament
D. By the President at will
e: The CEC is removed from office in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge — by an address of each House of Parliament supported by a majority of total membership and not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.

q: The Election Commission becomes multi-member when:
o: A. There are more than 3 candidates in any election
B. The President so appoints other Election Commissioners
C. Parliament passes a law for it
e: Article 324(2) provides that the Election Commission shall consist of the CEC and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may from time to time fix.

q: The Model Code of Conduct is:
o: A. An executive order under Article 77
C. A set of guidelines evolved by the Election Commission — not statutory, but binding in practice
D. A statutory document under Representation of People Act
e: The Model Code of Conduct is not a statutory document. It is a set of guidelines evolved by the Election Commission to regulate the conduct of political parties and candidates during elections. It derives force from Article 324.

q: In T.N. Seshan v. Union of India (1995), the Supreme Court held:
o: A. Election Commission cannot have multiple members
B. President's supervision over Election Commission is valid
C. Model Code of Conduct is legally binding
D. The CEC and other Election Commissioners have equal powers; CEC has no veto
e: The Supreme Court in T.N. Seshan (1995) held that all Election Commissioners have equal powers and the CEC does not have a veto over the other Commissioners. Decisions are taken by majority.

q: Which scholar defined Administrative Law as 'the law relating to the control of governmental power'?
e: H.W.R. Wade defined administrative law as 'the law relating to the control of governmental power.' Garner defined it as 'that branch of public law which is concerned with the composition, powers and duties of administrative authorities.'

q: A.V. Dicey was opposed to Administrative Law (Droit Administratif). His main objection was:
o: A. It was borrowed from French law
B. It gave too much power to courts
D. It created a separate system of law for government officials, violating Rule of Law
e: Dicey opposed Droit Administratif (French administrative law) because he believed in the Rule of Law which required every person, including government officials, to be subject to the same ordinary law of the land administered by ordinary courts. Concept note: Dicey's Rule of Law: Three meanings — (1) Supremacy of law; (2) Equality before the law — every man subject to ordinary law; (3) Constitution as a consequence of individual rights. Dicey was later corrected by Jennings and Wade who showed Droit Administratif actually protects citizens from the State.

q: The 'Droit Administratif' system of France is characterized by:
o: A. Complete immunity of the State from suit
B. Separate administrative courts (Conseil d'État) to deal with disputes involving the State
C. Courts using stare decisis in administrative decisions
D. Supremacy of ordinary civil courts
e: The French Droit Administratif system has a dual system of courts — ordinary courts for private law matters and separate administrative courts (headed by Conseil d'État) for disputes involving the State. France follows civil law tradition, not common law stare decisis.

q: Which of the following best describes delegated legislation?
o: B. Judicial precedent that creates law
C. Legislation made by executive bodies under authority conferred by Parliament
D. Legislation made by Parliament directly
e: Delegated (subordinate/subsidiary) legislation is law made by executive bodies (ministers, local authorities, statutory corporations) under specific authority conferred by an Act of Parliament. Concept note: Delegated Legislation: Parliament delegates legislative power to executive bodies to make rules/regulations/bye-laws. Subject to judicial review on grounds of: (1) ultra vires parent Act; (2) violation of FRs; (3) unreasonableness; (4) procedural defects. Key case: Delhi Laws Act Case (1951) — excessive delegation is unconstitutional.

q: The principle against 'excessive delegation' means:
o: A. Parliament cannot delegate at all
B. All delegated legislation is void
C. The executive can override parliamentary enactments
D. Parliament cannot abdicate itself — it must lay down policy; details only can be delegated
e: The doctrine of excessive delegation means Parliament must retain control by laying down the legislative policy and standards. Only the working out of details can be delegated. Leading case: In re Delhi Laws Act, AIR 1951 SC 332.

q: 'Ombudsman' concept originated in which country?
e: The concept of Ombudsman originated in Sweden in 1809. The Riksdag (Swedish Parliament) appointed the first Ombudsman to oversee the application of laws by officials. India's equivalent is Lokpal (Union) and Lokayukta (State).

q: Which Article of the Constitution is the basis for the 'State' being made accountable in administrative law?
e: Article 12 defines 'State' for the purposes of Part III (Fundamental Rights). It includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India.

q: In Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002), the Supreme Court laid down the test for a body to be 'State' under Article 12 as:
o: A. Whether the body receives grants
B. Functional control and financial dependence on government — 'instrumentality or agency of State'
C. Whether the body is a statutory corporation
e: In Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002), a 7-judge bench overruled Sabhajit Tewary v. Union of India and established the 'functional test' — a body is 'State' if it is an instrumentality or agency of the State based on factors like financial dependence, functional control, and whether the functions are of public importance.

q: The two main rules of Natural Justice are:
o: A. Audi alteram partem and Res judicata
B. Nemo judex and Stare decisis
C. Nemo debet esse judex in propria causa and Audi alteram partem
D. Audi alteram partem and Nemo tenetur
e: The two pillars of natural justice are: (1) Nemo debet esse judex in propria sua causa — no one shall be a judge in his own cause (rule against bias); (2) Audi alteram partem — hear the other side (right to fair hearing).

q: 'Nemo debet esse judex in propria sua causa' means:
o: A. Right to a fair hearing
B. Both parties must be heard
C. No one shall be a judge in his own cause — Rule against bias
D. The decision must be a speaking order
e: This maxim means that a person who has an interest in the outcome of a decision should not be the one to make that decision. It is the foundation of the rule against bias in natural justice.

q: Which case is regarded as the leading English authority on the rule against bias (pecuniary interest)?
o: B. Dimes v. Grand Junction Canal (1852)
e: In Dimes v. Grand Junction Canal (1852), Lord Chancellor held shares in the canal company. His decree was set aside even though there was no actual bias — pecuniary interest causes automatic disqualification. Concept note: Types of Bias: (1) Pecuniary bias — automatic disqualification (Dimes); (2) Personal bias — some connection with a party; (3) Subject matter bias — pre-judgment; (4) Departmental bias — decision-maker is part of the same department. Test in India: 'Real danger' or 'Reasonable suspicion' of bias — A.K. Kraipak (1970).

q: The leading case that revived the rules of natural justice and held they apply even to administrative decisions affecting rights or legitimate expectations is:
o: B. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
D. A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1970)
e: Before Ridge v. Baldwin (1964), natural justice was confined to strictly judicial or quasi-judicial functions. The House of Lords overturned this narrow view and held that natural justice applies wherever rights are affected.

q: In A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1970), the Supreme Court held that:
o: A. Natural justice principles apply to administrative functions also — distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial is obsolete
B. Government servants have no right to be heard
C. Natural justice applies only to judicial tribunals
D. The selection committee was validly constituted
e: In A.K. Kraipak (1970), a member of the selection committee was also a candidate. The SC held that natural justice principles apply to administrative functions as well — the boundary between judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative has become thin.

q: The doctrine of 'Legitimate Expectation' in administrative law means:
o: A. A person has a reasonable expectation based on previous practice, promise, or policy that procedural fairness will be observed before adverse action
B. A citizen can legitimately claim a Constitutional right
D. The expectation of winning a case
e: Legitimate Expectation arises when a public authority has made a representation (by conduct, policy, or promise) that creates a reasonable expectation in a person's mind that they will be heard before being adversely affected. Leading cases: GCHQ Case (1985 UK); Navjyoti Coop. v. Union of India (1992 India).

q: 'Speaking Order' requirement in natural justice means:
o: A. The decision must be made in open court
B. Orders must be announced orally
C. The affected party must be given an opportunity to speak
D. The decision-maker must record reasons for the decision
e: A 'speaking order' or 'reasoned order' is one where the authority records its reasons for the decision. Leading case in India: Bhagat Raja v. Union of India (1967) — quasi-judicial orders must be reasoned orders.

q: Which of the following is NOT an element of 'audi alteram partem'?
o: A. Right to be represented by a lawyer in all proceedings
B. Notice of the charge/case against the party
D. Opportunity to file a written reply
e: Right to legal representation is not an absolute requirement of audi alteram partem. It may or may not be required depending on the nature of proceedings and statutory provisions. The other three options are core components of the right to fair hearing.

q: The rule of natural justice can be excluded by:
o: A. Express statutory provision or necessary implication
e: Natural justice can be excluded by: (1) express statutory provision; (2) necessary implication from statute; (3) urgency/emergency where prior hearing is impossible; (4) impracticability. However, exclusion must be justified and must not violate Fundamental Rights.

q: In Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. A.P. State Road Transport Corp. (1959), the Supreme Court held:
o: A. The government need not give reasons for nationalisation
C. Natural justice is not applicable to economic regulation
D. An officer who heard objections to a scheme cannot himself sanction it — investigator cannot be adjudicator
e: In Gullapalli Nageswara Rao (1959), the SC held that the Secretary who had heard the objections to a road transport nationalization scheme could not himself sanction it — this violated natural justice as he would be judging his own hearing.

q: 'Institutional bias' or 'Departmental bias' arises when:
o: A. The whole department/institution has a pre-determined stance likely to influence the adjudicator
B. The judge personally knows the parties
C. The judge has pecuniary interest
e: Departmental or institutional bias arises when the adjudicator belongs to the same department whose policy or decision is being challenged. The environment itself creates a bias. Discussed in Gullapalli Nageswara Rao and State of U.P. v. Mohd. Nooh (1958).

q: Can the principle of natural justice be waived?
o: A. Yes — if the party with the right knowingly and voluntarily waives it
C. Never — it is a mandatory requirement
D. Only by the Supreme Court
e: Natural justice rights can be waived by the person entitled to them, provided the waiver is voluntary, knowing, and unambiguous. This is a well-established principle in both English and Indian administrative law.

q: The maxim 'Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done' is associated with:
e: This famous dictum was laid down by Lord Hewart CJ in R v. Sussex Justices (1924). It underpins the rule against bias — not only must actual bias be absent, but the appearance of bias must also be eliminated.

q: The doctrine of 'Post-decisional hearing' — giving opportunity to be heard after the decision — is:
o: A. Generally not a valid substitute for pre-decisional hearing; courts look at circumstances
B. Completely valid and satisfies natural justice always
C. Required in all administrative decisions
e: Post-decisional hearing is generally not an adequate substitute for a pre-decisional hearing. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court held that impounding a passport without prior hearing was invalid even though subsequent remedies were available.

q: 'Certiorari' is a writ that:
o: A. Restrains a person from acting in a particular way
B. Asks why a person should not be produced before a court
C. Commands a person to do a public duty
D. Brings up the record of a lower tribunal to a superior court to quash the decision
e: Certiorari is issued by a superior court to an inferior tribunal to remove proceedings and quash them if the inferior tribunal has acted without jurisdiction, in excess of jurisdiction, in violation of natural justice, or there is an error apparent on the face of the record.

q: 'Mandamus' as a writ is issued when:
o: A. A court certifies a question to a higher court
B. A decision needs to be quashed
C. There is an illegal detention
D. A public authority fails to perform its public duty
e: Mandamus (Latin: 'we command') is issued by a superior court to a public authority, official, corporation, or lower court directing them to perform a public duty which they have failed or refused to perform.

q: Under what circumstances is the writ of Habeas Corpus issued?
o: A. To quash an illegal order
B. To compel performance of a public duty
C. To direct production of a detained person before court to examine legality of detention
D. To restrain a court from exceeding its jurisdiction
e: Habeas Corpus (Latin: 'you have the body') is the most important writ for protection of individual liberty. It requires the detaining authority to produce the detained person before the court so the court can determine the legality of the detention.

q: The grounds of judicial review in English law were authoritatively classified into three categories in which case?
o: A. Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for Civil Service — GCHQ Case (1985)
B. Anisminic v. Foreign Compensation Commission (1969)
C. Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948)
e: Lord Diplock in the GCHQ Case (1985) classified the grounds of judicial review into three categories: (1) Illegality; (2) Irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness); (3) Procedural Impropriety. Concept note: Lord Diplock's Three Grounds (GCHQ Case, 1985): (1) Illegality — decision-maker must understand and act within the law; (2) Irrationality — decision so unreasonable no reasonable authority could have made it (Wednesbury); (3) Procedural Impropriety — failure to observe statutory procedures or natural justice. A 4th ground — Proportionality — is now recognized in EU/Human Rights contexts.

q: 'Wednesbury unreasonableness' refers to:
o: A. A decision made without jurisdiction
B. A decision against natural justice
C. A decision so outrageous in its defiance of logic or accepted moral standards that no sensible person could have arrived at it
D. A decision that is slightly wrong
e: Wednesbury unreasonableness comes from Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223, where Lord Greene MR described it as a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it.

q: The doctrine of 'Ultra Vires' in administrative law means:
o: C. Acting beyond the powers granted by the enabling statute
D. Acting within the granted powers
e: Ultra vires (Latin: 'beyond powers') means acting outside the scope of authority granted. Two types: (1) Substantive ultra vires — acting beyond the scope of powers; (2) Procedural ultra vires — failing to follow prescribed procedures.

q: 'Proportionality' as a ground of judicial review requires that:
o: A. The decision must be proportionate to the resources available
B. The means adopted must be proportionate to the end sought — fair balance between individual rights and public interest
C. Punishment must be proportionate to the offence in criminal cases only
D. Administrative decisions must be made within a proportionate time
e: Proportionality requires a fair balance between the means used and the end sought. It is stricter than Wednesbury unreasonableness. Recognised in India in Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001). Courts examine whether a less restrictive means could achieve the same result.

q: Judicial review of administrative action in India is primarily based on:
o: A. Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution
e: Judicial review of administrative action in India primarily flows from Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts) through the writ jurisdiction. It is a constitutional power, not merely a statutory one.

q: The doctrine of 'Legitimate Expectation' as a ground of judicial review was first clearly expounded in Indian law in:
o: A. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
B. Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing Society v. Union of India (1992)
C. A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India
D. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
e: The doctrine of Legitimate Expectation was clearly expounded in Indian administrative law in Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing Society v. Union of India (1992), where the SC held that a change in policy without giving an opportunity to be heard violated legitimate expectation.

q: 'Mala fide' (bad faith) as a ground of judicial review implies:
o: A. The authority acted with personal animosity or improper purpose
B. The authority had no jurisdiction
D. The authority made a technical error
e: Mala fide or bad faith as a ground of judicial review means the authority exercised its power for an improper purpose, with personal animosity, or in abuse of power. Courts are very slow to impute mala fides — it must be clearly established.

q: 'Error apparent on the face of the record' as a ground of certiorari means:
o: A. Any error in the decision
B. Only an error so obvious and manifest that it does not require elaborate reasoning to detect
e: Error apparent on the face of the record must be clear and manifest without requiring detailed argument or examination of evidence. Established in Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan (1964 SC).

q: In Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission (1969) [HL], the House of Lords held:
o: A. Natural justice cannot apply to tribunals
B. The Commission had acted within its powers
C. Certiorari does not lie against statutory tribunals
D. Any error of law (not just jurisdictional error in the old technical sense) makes a decision a nullity
e: Anisminic (1969) effectively abolished the old distinction between 'jurisdictional error' (always reviewable) and 'error within jurisdiction' (not reviewable by certiorari). The HL held that any error of law goes to jurisdiction and makes the decision a nullity.

q: The 'Doctrine of Proportionality' in Indian administrative law was specifically adopted in:
o: A. Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001)
B. Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985)
C. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
D. Saraswathi v. Union of India (1999)
e: In Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001), the Supreme Court specifically adopted the doctrine of proportionality in Indian administrative law for reviewing punishments imposed on government servants.

q: Which Article provides for Administrative Tribunals to deal with service matters?
e: Article 323-A deals with Administrative Tribunals for service matters (inserted by 42nd Amendment, 1976; operationalized by Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985). Article 323-B provides for tribunals for other matters like taxation, elections, industrial disputes, etc.

q: Assertion (A): Article 21 includes the right to a fair trial and speedy justice. Reason (R): In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), the SC held speedy trial is a component of Article 21.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
B. Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation
C. A is true but R is false
D. A is false but R is true
e: Article 21 has been expansively interpreted to include the right to speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), right to legal aid, and right to fair procedure. R correctly explains why A is true.

q: Assertion (A): The President can promulgate an Ordinance under Article 123 only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session. Reason (R): An Ordinance ceases at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
B. Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation
C. A is true but R is false
D. A is false but R is true
e: A is true — Ordinance can be promulgated when at least one House of Parliament is not in session (not necessarily both). R is also true — 6 weeks maximum after reassembly. But R is the duration rule, not the explanation for when it can be issued.

q: Assertion (A): DPSPs are non-justiciable. Reason (R): They are fundamental in governance and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
B. Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
C. A is true but R is false
D. A is false but R is true
e: Both A (Article 37 — non-justiciable) and R (Article 37 — fundamental in governance) are true. However, R does not explain WHY they are non-justiciable. They are non-justiciable because of a deliberate constitutional design separating justiciable rights from non-justiciable policy guidelines.

q: Match the writs with their purpose: (i) Mandamus (ii) Habeas Corpus (iii) Prohibition (iv) Quo Warranto — (a) Release from illegal detention (b) Perform a public duty (c) Prevent inferior tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction (d) Question authority to hold public office
e: Mandamus (b) — compels performance of a public duty. Habeas Corpus (a) — secures release from illegal detention. Prohibition (c) — prevents inferior tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction (preventive). Quo Warranto (d) — questions by what authority a person holds a public office.

q: Match the Articles with their subjects: (i) Art.249 (ii) Art.352 (iii) Art.356 (iv) Art.360 — (a) Financial Emergency (b) Parliament legislates on State List in national interest (c) National Emergency (d) Failure of constitutional machinery in State
e: Article 249 (b) — Parliament legislates on State List in national interest via Rajya Sabha resolution. Article 352 (c) — National Emergency. Article 356 (d) — Failure of constitutional machinery/President's Rule. Article 360 (a) — Financial Emergency.

q: Which of the following is CORRECT about the 'Basic Structure Doctrine'? (i) Propounded in Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973); (ii) Limits Parliament's amending power; (iii) Federalism is a basic feature; (iv) Free and fair elections is a basic feature
o: B. i, ii and iii only
C. i, ii, iii and iv — all four correct
e: All four are correct: (i) Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established basic structure; (ii) Parliament cannot amend to destroy basic structure; (iii) Federal character is a basic structure element (Kesavananda); (iv) Free and fair elections recognised as basic structure in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).

q: The 'Doctrine of Eclipse' in Constitutional Law means:
o: A. A law void ab initio becomes valid retrospectively when the constitutional bar is removed
B. A pre-constitutional law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right becomes dormant/eclipsed (not void) and revives if the inconsistency is removed
C. A law is eclipsed by a subsequent constitutional amendment
e: The Doctrine of Eclipse applies to pre-constitutional laws. Such a law is not void ab initio — it is merely eclipsed/dormant to the extent of inconsistency. If the constitutional bar is removed (e.g., by amending the FR), the law revives. Leading case: Bhikhaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP (1955).

q: 'Res Judicata' in administrative law means:
o: A. Natural justice must be followed
B. A superior court can always review lower court decisions
C. No one can be a judge in his own case
D. A decided question between the same parties cannot be re-agitated
e: Res judicata (a matter already judged) means that once a matter is decided between the same parties on the same facts and the same cause of action by a competent court, it cannot be re-litigated. It applies in administrative law too.

q: Under Article 309, the conditions of service of persons serving the Union or States can be regulated by:
o: C. An Act of the appropriate legislature; until such Act is made, by executive rules
e: Article 309 enables the appropriate legislature (Parliament for Union; State Legislature for State) to regulate the recruitment and conditions of service. Until Parliament or the State Legislature makes such a law, the President or Governor may make rules.

q: The 'Doctrine of Pleasure' — Article 310 — means government servants hold office 'during the pleasure of the President/Governor.' This is subject to:
o: B. Article 311 — procedural safeguards of inquiry before dismissal/removal/reduction in rank
e: Article 310 establishes the doctrine of pleasure. But Article 311 provides constitutional safeguards: (1) No dismissal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority; (2) Reasonable opportunity to show cause before dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank.

q: Which of the following cases is associated with PIL being used to enforce Fundamental Rights of disadvantaged groups?
o: A. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984)
B. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (environmental law)
C. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
D. All of the above — PIL has been used in all these
e: PIL has been used in all these landmark cases: Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) — bonded labour; M.C. Mehta — environmental protection; Vishaka (1997) — sexual harassment at workplace. PIL through Articles 32/226 has become a powerful tool for social justice.

q: Under the original Constitution, a National Emergency could be proclaimed on the ground of 'internal disturbance.' Which Amendment replaced this with 'armed rebellion'?
e: The 44th Amendment (1978) substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance' in Article 352. This made it harder to impose emergency for mere civil unrest — a direct response to the misuse during the 1975 Emergency.

q: The National Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on the ground of:
o: B. Threat of war with China
D. Internal disturbance — the first and only such proclamation on internal grounds
e: The National Emergency proclaimed on June 25, 1975 was the only emergency declared on the ground of internal disturbance (now 'armed rebellion'). Earlier emergencies (1962, 1965, 1971) were on grounds of external aggression/war.

q: Under Article 352(3), a proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by each House of Parliament by:
o: A. Absolute majority of total membership of each House
D. Special majority — not less than 2/3 of members present and voting AND a majority of total membership
e: Article 352(6) requires special majority for approval of National Emergency proclamation: not less than two-thirds of members of each House present and voting, which must also be a majority of the total membership of each House.

q: The maximum initial period for which a National Emergency can operate without Parliamentary approval is:
e: Under Article 352(4), the proclamation of National Emergency must be laid before each House of Parliament and ceases to operate at the expiration of one month unless approved before that. After approval, it continues for 6 months.

q: Once approved, a National Emergency continues for what period and how is it renewed?
o: C. 6 months — must be renewed every 6 months by special majority
D. Until revoked, with no renewal requirement
e: After initial Parliamentary approval, the National Emergency continues for 6 months. For each subsequent 6-month period, fresh approval by special majority is required.

q: A National Emergency can be revoked by the President:
o: A. On his own initiative OR on a resolution passed by Lok Sabha by simple majority — Article 352(7) & (8)
B. By the Supreme Court order
e: Under Article 352(8), if a notice is signed by not less than 1/10 of total members of Lok Sabha, a special sitting must be held within 14 days. If the House passes a resolution by simple majority disapproving the Emergency, the President must revoke it. This is the only instance where Lok Sabha alone can act constitutionally. Concept note: Lok Sabha Revocation: Article 352(8) gives the Lok Sabha alone the unique power to disapprove a National Emergency by simple majority — this is an exception to the general rule that both Houses must act together on constitutional matters.

q: During a National Emergency (war/external aggression), Article 358 suspends Article 19 rights:
o: A. On Presidential order specifying which rights
B. Only in affected border states
C. Automatically but only as regards laws inconsistent with Article 19 made during Emergency
D. Automatically and absolutely for the duration
e: Article 358 operates automatically during war/external aggression emergency but only saves laws MADE DURING the Emergency. Pre-existing laws that violate Article 19 are not automatically saved by Article 358.

q: Article 359 differs from Article 358 in that:
o: A. Article 359 relates to financial emergency only
B. Article 359 requires a Presidential Order specifying which FRs (other than Arts. 20 & 21) can be suspended — it is not automatic
D. Article 359 applies only to internal emergency
e: Article 358 operates automatically (only for Art. 19, only during war/external aggression). Article 359 requires the President to issue an Order specifying which Fundamental Rights (excluding Arts. 20 & 21) shall not be enforceable. It is discretionary and specific.

q: Which Articles of the Constitution CANNOT be suspended even during National Emergency by Presidential Order under Article 359?
e: The 44th Amendment, 1978 amended Article 359 to exclude Articles 20 and 21 from the President's power to suspend enforcement of Fundamental Rights during Emergency. Articles 20 (protection from ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination) and 21 (right to life) can NEVER be suspended.

q: Article 20 protects against:
o: D. Ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination
e: Article 20 provides triple protection: (1) No ex post facto criminal law — no person convicted of offence which was not an offence when committed; (2) No double jeopardy — no person prosecuted and punished more than once for the same offence; (3) No self-incrimination — no person compelled to be a witness against himself.

q: During a National Emergency, Parliament acquires power to legislate on:
o: B. Both Union List and State List subjects — Article 250
C. All three Lists with extra powers
e: Under Article 250, while a proclamation of National Emergency is in operation, Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter in the State List. This extends Parliamentary legislative power significantly during Emergency.

q: During National Emergency, the President can modify constitutional provisions relating to distribution of revenues under:
e: Article 354 enables the President to direct that all or any provisions of Articles 268–279 (dealing with distribution of revenues between Union and States) shall apply with modifications or exceptions during a National Emergency.

q: The maximum period for which President's Rule can operate without fresh Parliamentary approval is:
e: A proclamation under Article 356 must be approved by Parliament within 2 months. Once approved, it operates for 6 months. It can be renewed every 6 months up to a maximum of 3 years (beyond 1 year only with special conditions under Article 356(4) & (5)).

q: Under Article 356, President's Rule beyond ONE YEAR requires, in addition to Parliamentary approval:
o: B. Both (A) or (B) — either condition must be satisfied
C. A recommendation by the Election Commission that elections cannot be held in that State
D. A declaration of National Emergency in the whole of India or the concerned State
e: Article 356(4) and (5) provide that beyond one year, President's Rule can only be extended if either: (a) a National Emergency is in operation in the whole or part of the concerned State; OR (b) the Election Commission certifies that elections to the Legislative Assembly of the State cannot be held.

q: The absolute maximum period for which President's Rule can be imposed in a State is:
e: President's Rule under Article 356 can be imposed for a maximum of 3 years. After 3 years, fresh elections must be held. Extension beyond 1 year requires special conditions under Article 356(4) & (5).

q: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the Proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review on which ground?
o: A. President has no discretion in issuing it
B. Mala fide exercise or based on wholly irrelevant grounds — courts can examine the material
D. It is void unless confirmed by Supreme Court
e: S.R. Bommai (1994) — 9-judge bench held: (1) Art. 356 proclamation is justiciable; (2) President cannot dissolve Assembly until Parliament approves (suspended animation); (3) Secularism is basic structure; (4) Floor of the House is the sole test of majority; (5) Courts can examine whether material before President was relevant. Concept note: S.R. Bommai (1994) is one of the most important cases on federalism. It effectively curtailed arbitrary use of Article 356 and upheld federalism as a basic structure of the Constitution.

q: 'Suspended animation' of State Legislative Assembly during President's Rule means:
o: A. The Assembly is dissolved immediately
B. The Assembly is dissolved after 6 months
C. The Assembly is neither dissolved nor allowed to function — kept in suspended state pending Parliamentary approval
e: S.R. Bommai held that until Parliament approves the proclamation under Article 356, the President cannot dissolve the State Legislative Assembly. It is put in 'suspended animation' — neither dissolved nor operative. If Parliament disapproves, the Assembly revives.

q: Financial Emergency under Article 360 can be proclaimed when:
o: A. A State refuses to pay taxes
B. GDP falls below a threshold
C. There is a balance of payments crisis
D. The financial stability of India or any part thereof is threatened
e: Article 360 provides that the President may proclaim a Financial Emergency if he is satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened.

q: During Financial Emergency, the President can direct reduction of salaries and allowances of:
o: B. All government servants including Supreme Court and High Court judges
e: Article 360(4)(b) uniquely allows reduction of salaries and allowances of all persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union including the judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts during Financial Emergency. Financial Emergency has never been proclaimed in India.

q: Under Article 356, which of the following powers does the President NOT acquire during President's Rule?
o: A. Power to dissolve the High Court of the State
B. Power to suspend constitutional provisions relating to any body in the State
C. Power to declare that Parliament can legislate on State List subjects
D. Power to assume functions of State government
e: During President's Rule, the President takes over the executive functions of the State government and Parliament can legislate on State subjects. However, the High Courts continue to function — they are constitutional courts established under Articles 214-231 and are not affected by Article 356.

q: The Governor is appointed by the President under Article 155. The Governor's term of office is:
o: C. Co-terminus with the State government
D. 5 years or during the pleasure of the President — whichever is earlier
e: Article 156(1) provides that the Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. Article 156(3) provides that the Governor shall hold office for a term of 5 years from the date of entering upon office — subject to the pleasure of the President.

q: Which of the following is a discretionary power of the Governor NOT requiring Council of Ministers' advice?
o: A. Appointment of Chief Minister when no party has clear majority
B. Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President — Article 200
C. Giving assent to a Bill
e: The Governor's discretionary powers include: (1) Appointment of CM when no clear majority; (2) Dismissal of CoM which has lost majority but refuses to resign; (3) Dissolution of State Assembly in certain situations; (4) Reservation of Bills; (5) Seeking information from CM under Article 167. All others require CoM advice. Concept note: Governor's Discretionary Powers (Article 163(2)): These are exercised without CoM advice: Appointment of CM when no clear majority, Dismissal of CoM that has lost majority, Dissolution of Assembly (contested), Reservation of Bills for Presidential consideration, Seeking information from CM (Art. 167), Sending Art. 356 report.

q: Under Article 167, the Chief Minister is under a duty to:
o: A. Report Cabinet decisions to Parliament
B. Report all Cabinet decisions to the President
C. Communicate to the Governor all decisions of the Council of Ministers and proposals for legislation
D. Seek Governor's prior approval for all Cabinet decisions
e: Article 167 imposes three duties on the Chief Minister: (1) to communicate to the Governor all decisions of CoM relating to administration of the State; (2) to furnish information relating to administration of the State and proposals for legislation as the Governor may call for; (3) if the Governor requires, to submit for consideration of CoM any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister.

q: Under Article 200, can the Governor give assent, withhold assent, or return a Bill passed by the State Legislature?
o: A. Only Money Bills can be returned
B. Yes — Governor may assent, withhold, or return (non-money bill) for reconsideration; if re-passed, must give assent
C. No — must always give assent
D. Yes — Governor can withhold assent permanently
e: Article 200 gives the Governor four options: (1) give assent; (2) withhold assent; (3) return (non-Money Bill) for reconsideration; (4) reserve for President's consideration. Crucially, if the State Legislature re-passes the Bill with or without amendments, the Governor MUST give assent.

q: When a Governor reserves a Bill for the President's consideration under Article 200, the President under Article 201 may:
o: A. Give or withhold assent only
B. Give assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it for reconsideration
C. Return it; if re-passed, President must assent
D. Both B and C — President has wider discretion than Governor
e: Under Article 201, the President has full discretion — he may give assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return the Bill for reconsideration. Unlike the Governor (who MUST assent if a Bill is re-passed), the President is NOT bound to assent even if the State Legislature re-passes it.

q: Under Article 213, the Governor can promulgate Ordinances when:
o: A. The State Legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary
B. State Legislature is in recess only
C. There is a law and order situation only
D. The Governor deems it fit at any time
e: Article 213 empowers the Governor to promulgate Ordinances when the State Legislature is not in session (or both Houses of a bicameral legislature) and the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist that render immediate action necessary.

q: An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor ceases to operate if:
o: A. Not approved by the State Legislature within 6 weeks of its reassembly
B. A resolution disapproving it is passed by either House
C. Both A and B, or if the Governor revokes it
D. Only if the Governor revokes it
e: Under Article 213(2), an Ordinance ceases to operate: (1) at the expiry of 6 weeks after reassembly of the Legislature; (2) if before that, a resolution disapproving it is passed; (3) if the Governor withdraws it at any time.

q: The Governor's pardoning power under Article 161 versus the President's power under Article 72 — which statement is CORRECT?
o: A. Governor's power extends to sentences of death awarded under State laws
B. Governor CANNOT pardon a death sentence — that is exclusively President's power
C. Governor pardons all offences including military offences
D. Both have identical pardoning powers
e: Article 161 gives the Governor power to grant pardons for offences against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends. Article 72 gives the President the power to pardon death sentences, court martial offences, and offences against Union laws. Governor has NO power over death sentences.

q: In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the Supreme Court held on the role of the Governor that:
o: A. The Governor can appoint and dismiss Ministers independently
B. The Governor, like the President, is a constitutional head who acts on CoM advice in all matters except where Constitution expressly provides for discretion
C. The Governor has overriding power over the State Council of Ministers
D. The Governor acts entirely on personal discretion in all matters
e: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) — 7-judge bench — held that both the President and Governor are constitutional heads bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers except where the Constitution expressly confers discretionary powers. This is the foundational case on constitutional conventions regarding executive heads.

q: The Governor's report recommending imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 is:
o: A. Subject to Rajya Sabha approval first
D. Not binding — President acts on Union Cabinet's advice, not solely on Governor's report
e: The Governor's report is the 'occasion' for invoking Article 356, but the decision is made by the Union Cabinet and the President acts on Cabinet's advice. The President is not bound by the Governor's report. S.R. Bommai held that the courts can examine the material on which President was satisfied.

q: A person to be appointed as Governor must satisfy which qualifications?
o: A. Be nominated by the concerned State Legislature
B. Be a retired judge of the Supreme Court
C. Be a citizen of India aged not less than 30 years
D. Be a citizen of India aged not less than 35 years
e: Article 157 prescribes that a person shall not be eligible for appointment as Governor unless he is a citizen of India and has completed the age of 35 years. Article 158 adds that he must not be a member of either House of Parliament or State Legislature and must not hold any office of profit.

q: The Governor enjoys personal immunity from legal proceedings under Article 361. This immunity covers:
o: A. Only official acts done in exercise of powers and duties
C. For 2 years after leaving office
D. Official acts AND personal acts during tenure — complete immunity
e: Article 361 provides: (1) The President/Governor shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise of his powers; (2) No criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted against them during their tenure; (3) No civil proceedings for acts done in personal capacity without 2 months' notice.

q: In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court:
o: A. Held the Governor's action was valid but ordered fresh elections
B. Held that the Governor can dissolve Assembly without any reason
C. Struck down the premature dissolution of Bihar Assembly by the Governor as mala fide
D. Upheld the dissolution of Bihar Assembly by the Governor
e: In Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the SC struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Legislative Assembly before its first session as unconstitutional and mala fide. The Governor had acted on incorrect advice and in a politically motivated manner.

q: In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held regarding removal of Governors:
o: A. The power to remove a Governor cannot be exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or for extraneous reasons — Governor must be given opportunity to be heard
B. The President can remove a Governor at will for any reason
C. A Governor cannot be removed before 5 years
D. Removal of Governor requires Parliamentary approval
e: In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the SC held that while the President can remove a Governor under Article 156(1) (pleasure doctrine), this power cannot be exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or for political reasons. The Governor must be given an opportunity to present their case.

q: Under Article 111, if the President returns a Bill to Parliament and Parliament re-passes it with or without amendment, the President:
o: A. Shall NOT withhold assent — must sign the Bill
C. Can reserve it for the Supreme Court's opinion
e: Article 111 provides that if the Bill is re-passed by both Houses with or without amendments, the President shall not withhold assent. This provision makes the President's veto a suspensive veto, not an absolute veto.

q: The Vice President of India is elected by:
o: A. Same electoral college as President
B. Elected members of both Houses of Parliament
C. Members of both Houses of Parliament — elected AND nominated
D. Elected members of Rajya Sabha only
e: Under Article 66, the Vice President is elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament — both elected AND nominated members. This is broader than the President's electoral college which includes only elected members.

q: The Vice President acts as the ex-officio Chairman of which House?
o: C. Both Houses on alternate days
D. Neither — only when President is absent
e: Article 64 provides that the Vice-President shall be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). The Speaker is the presiding officer of the Lok Sabha.

q: Under Article 65, the Vice President acts as President when:
o: A. A vacancy arises in the office of the President or the President is unable to discharge functions
C. The Prime Minister is absent
e: Article 65(1) — VP discharges functions of President during casual vacancies. Article 65(2) — VP acts as President during absence/inability of the President. The VP can act only until the President resumes duty or a new President is elected.

q: The President of India can seek the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court under:
e: Article 143 empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion. The SC's opinion is advisory and not binding on the President, but has great persuasive value.

q: Under Article 72, the President's pardoning power extends to:
o: A. Only cases where appeal is pending
B. All cases of conviction including State law offences
C. Only Supreme Court convicted persons
D. Cases involving offences against Union laws and death sentences
e: Article 72 gives the President power to grant pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, or commutation of punishment to persons convicted of: (1) offences against Union laws; (2) offences by court martial; (3) all sentences of death. The Governor's pardoning power (Art. 161) covers State law offences but NOT death sentences or court martial.

q: The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha after the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 is:
e: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 abolished the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. The maximum strength of Lok Sabha is now 543 elected members.

q: The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is:
e: Article 80 provides that the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) shall consist of not more than 238 representatives of States and Union Territories (elected) and 12 nominated by the President for their expertise in literature, science, art, and social service. Maximum = 250.

q: Under Article 110, a Bill is a Money Bill if it contains ONLY provisions dealing with:
o: A. Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any tax
B. Appropriation of moneys from the Consolidated Fund
C. Borrowing of money by the Government
D. All of the above among other specified matters in Art. 110(1)
e: Article 110(1) defines a Money Bill as a Bill containing ONLY provisions dealing with matters specified in clauses (a) to (g), including: (a) imposition/abolition/remission/alteration/regulation of tax; (b) regulation of borrowing; (c) custody of Consolidated Fund; (d) appropriation from Consolidated Fund; (e) supplementary expenditure; (f) audit accounts; (g) any incidental matter.

q: A Money Bill can be introduced only in:
o: A. A joint sitting of Parliament
e: Article 109 provides that a Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). It must be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within 14 days — Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.

q: Parliamentary privilege under Article 105 includes:
o: A. Freedom of speech in Parliament
B. Right not to be arrested in civil cases during session and 40 days before/after
e: Article 105 privileges include: (1) Freedom of speech in Parliament — MPs cannot be sued for anything said in Parliament; (2) No arrest in civil cases during session + 40 days before and after. Key case: Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024) — 7-judge bench held that bribe-taking MPs have NO immunity under Article 105, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998). Concept note: Parliamentary Privileges: Article 105(2) — no Member liable for anything said or vote given in Parliament. The court cannot question Parliamentary proceedings. Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024) is the latest landmark — MPs who take bribes to vote are NOT protected.

q: A joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108 CANNOT be convened for which Bills?
o: A. Money Bills and Constitutional Amendment Bills
e: Joint sitting under Article 108 is only for ordinary Bills on which there is a deadlock. Money Bills cannot go to joint sitting (they are exclusively Lok Sabha's domain). Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368 must be passed by each House separately by special majority — no joint sitting.

q: The 'Anti-Defection Law' is contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
e: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. It provides for disqualification of members on grounds of defection. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the 'split' exception, retaining only 'merger' (2/3 members joining another party).

q: Under the Tenth Schedule, a Member of the Legislature is disqualified for defection if:
o: A. He voluntarily gives up membership of his political party OR votes contrary to party direction without prior permission and without being condoned within 15 days
B. He is absent during any vote
C. He votes against his party's direction on any vote
D. He criticizes his party leader publicly
e: Under the Tenth Schedule, a member is disqualified if: (1) he voluntarily gives up membership of his political party; (2) he votes or abstains in contravention of any direction issued by his party without prior permission and the party has not condoned it within 15 days.

q: The Ninth Schedule of the Constitution was introduced by which Amendment and for what purpose?
o: B. First Constitutional Amendment, 1951 — to protect land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenge
C. Original Constitution — to protect land reform laws
e: The Ninth Schedule was inserted by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 to protect certain land reform laws from being challenged on the ground of violation of Fundamental Rights. Key case: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) — laws in 9th Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda) can be challenged if they violate basic structure.

q: Under Article 368, which constitutional provisions require ratification by not less than half of the State Legislatures?
o: A. Federal provisions — Art. 54, 55, 73, 162, Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, Art. 368 itself
e: Article 368 provides three categories of amendment: (1) Simple majority — matters like creation of new States; (2) Special majority (2/3 + majority of total) — most provisions; (3) Special majority + ratification by not less than half of State Legislatures — federal provisions affecting Centre-State relations.

q: The 'Doctrine of Occupied Field' in legislative relations means:
o: A. Only Union can occupy Concurrent List
B. When Parliament intends to cover the entire field on a Concurrent List subject, there is no scope for State legislation
C. States cannot legislate at all on Concurrent subjects
D. When Parliament legislates on a Concurrent List subject, the State law is automatically repealed
e: The Doctrine of Occupied Field operates under Article 254. When Parliament's law is intended to be exhaustive and covers the entire field of a Concurrent List subject, a State law on the same subject is repugnant to the extent it encroaches on the occupied field.

q: Under Article 262, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of:
e: Article 262 enables Parliament to provide by law for the adjudication of disputes relating to the waters of inter-State rivers and river valleys, and to exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. The Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 creates specific tribunals for this purpose.

q: The Sarkaria Commission (1988) on Centre-State relations recommended:
o: B. The Governor's role should be increased
C. Finance Commission recommendations should be made binding
D. Inter-State Council should be revived and made a permanent body for Union-State coordination
e: The Sarkaria Commission (1988) made comprehensive recommendations on Centre-State relations including: revival of Inter-State Council; restraint in use of Article 356; appointment of persons with standing in State as Governor; Governor to follow conventions. The Punchhi Commission (2010) also made similar recommendations.

q: Under Article 365, if any State fails to comply with Union directions, the President may treat it as:
o: C. A breakdown of constitutional machinery — triggering Article 356
e: Article 365 provides that where any State has failed to comply with or give effect to any direction given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution — thus enabling Art. 356.

q: The Finance Commission is constituted under which Article?
e: Article 280 provides that the President shall, within two years from the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary, constitute a Finance Commission to recommend distribution of tax revenues.

q: Which of the following is in the Union List (List I, Seventh Schedule)?
e: Defence of India is Entry 1 of the Union List. Public order and Police are in the State List (List II). Agriculture is in the State List (Entry 14). Education is in the Concurrent List (Entry 25, after 42nd Amendment).

q: 'Education' was originally in which List? After which Amendment was it moved to the Concurrent List?
o: A. State List; moved to Concurrent List by 42nd Amendment, 1976
C. Union List; moved by 44th Amendment
D. State List; moved by 86th Amendment
e: Originally, 'Education' was in the State List (List II). The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 shifted 'Education' including universities to Entry 25 of the Concurrent List, enabling both Parliament and State Legislatures to legislate on it.

q: Under Article 256, the executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure:
o: A. Compliance with Union laws made by Parliament
B. Compliance with Supreme Court orders
C. Compliance with Finance Commission recommendations
e: Article 256 imposes a mandatory obligation on States to exercise their executive power so as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws that apply in the State. The Union may give necessary directions to the State for this purpose.

q: The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President in consultation with:
o: A. Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State — Article 217
B. Chief Justice of India only
D. The State Council of Ministers
e: Article 217 provides that the Chief Justice of a High Court shall be appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State. For other HC judges, the Chief Justice of the concerned HC is also consulted.

q: A High Court judge holds office until:
o: B. The pleasure of the President
e: Article 217(1) provides that a Judge of a High Court shall hold office until he attains the age of 62 years. Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years under Article 124(2).
