q: The power of a High Court to transfer cases from subordinate courts involving substantial constitutional questions is provided under:
e: Article 228 provides that if the High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, it may withdraw the case and either dispose of it itself or determine the question and return the case.

q: Which of the following is CORRECT about High Courts' writ jurisdiction under Article 226?
o: A. It is exactly the same as Article 32
B. It can only be used against State government
C. It is narrower than SC's writ jurisdiction under Article 32
D. It is wider than Article 32 — can be used for enforcement of any legal right, not just FRs
e: Article 226 is wider than Article 32 in two respects: (1) It can be used for enforcement of any legal right, not just Fundamental Rights; (2) High Courts can issue writs against any person or authority within their territorial jurisdiction. However, Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, unlike Article 226.

q: The concept of 'Territorial Jurisdiction' of High Courts for writ petitions means:
o: A. Any HC in India has jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights violations
B. Only domicile of the petitioner matters
C. Writs can only be filed in the State where the petitioner resides
D. The cause of action must arise or the respondent must be located within the HC's territorial jurisdiction
e: Under Article 226, the High Court can issue writs to any person or authority within the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction. If any part of the cause of action arises within the HC's territorial jurisdiction, it has jurisdiction. This is especially important for petitions against Central Government.

q: 'Prohibition' writ differs from 'Certiorari' in that:
o: A. Both are issued only after the decision
B. There is no difference — both quash decisions
C. Certiorari is preventive; Prohibition is curative
D. Prohibition is issued before the inferior tribunal makes its decision; Certiorari is issued after to quash it
e: Prohibition is a preventive writ — issued to an inferior tribunal to stop it from exceeding jurisdiction before it makes a decision. Certiorari is a curative writ — issued after a decision to bring the record to a superior court and quash it. Both deal with jurisdictional excess.

q: 'Quo Warranto' writ can be issued against:
o: A. Any person performing any duty
B. A person holding a public office without legal authority or against a person claiming a public office
e: Quo Warranto (Latin: 'by what authority') questions the authority by which a person holds a public office. It can be issued against a person who claims or usurps a public office. Leading case: University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao (1964). It is a discretionary writ, not a writ of right.

q: Which of the following CANNOT be enforced through a writ of Mandamus?
o: A. A statutory duty of a public authority
B. A duty to follow natural justice
D. A discretionary duty where authority refuses to exercise discretion at all
e: Mandamus is issued only to enforce PUBLIC duties — statutory or constitutional. It cannot enforce purely private contractual rights. However, if a public authority refuses to exercise its discretion altogether (as opposed to exercising it wrongly), mandamus can compel it to act.

q: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established under:
o: A. Article 323-A and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
e: Article 323-A (inserted by 42nd Amendment, 1976) provides for Administrative Tribunals for adjudication of disputes relating to recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed to public services. The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 operationalized this provision by establishing the CAT.

q: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held:
o: A. Only Supreme Court can review CAT decisions
B. Administrative Tribunals Act is unconstitutional
C. Power of High Courts under Articles 226/227 cannot be excluded — it is part of the basic structure
D. CAT is the final authority on service matters
e: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), a 7-judge Constitutional Bench held that the power of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution and cannot be excluded even by a constitutional provision. CAT decisions are therefore subject to HC Division Bench review. Concept note: L. Chandra Kumar Principle: Judicial review by the High Court is a basic structure feature. Even the Constitution (through Art. 323-A(2)(d)) cannot validly exclude this jurisdiction. CAT functions as a court of first instance; its decisions go to HC Division Bench for judicial review.

q: 'Lokpal' under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 has jurisdiction over:
o: A. Only Central government employees below Joint Secretary level
B. Public servants including PM (with conditions), Ministers, MPs, Group A/B/C/D officials, and certain NGOs
e: Lokpal has jurisdiction over the Prime Minister (with significant restrictions — matters relating to external affairs, security, public order excluded), Union Ministers, Members of Parliament, Group A/B/C/D officers of Union, and officers of certain entities receiving government funding.

q: The Lokpal is headed by:
o: A. A sitting Supreme Court judge
B. A retired Chief Justice of India compulsorily
C. A person who is/has been CJI or a SC judge or an eminent person meeting prescribed criteria
e: The Lokpal Act, 2013 provides that the Chairperson shall be a person who is or has been the Chief Justice of India or a judge of the Supreme Court OR an eminent person of impeccable integrity and outstanding ability, having special knowledge and expertise of not less than 25 years in public administration.

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid ground for challenging delegated legislation in courts?
o: A. Procedural ultra vires — failure to follow mandatory consultation/publication
B. The parent Act itself was passed hastily by Parliament
C. Ultra vires the parent Act
e: Delegated legislation can be challenged on grounds of: (1) substantive ultra vires (beyond scope of parent Act); (2) violation of Fundamental Rights; (3) procedural ultra vires (failure to follow mandatory procedures); (4) unreasonableness; (5) sub-delegation without authority. The speed of passing the parent Act is NOT a ground for challenging subordinate legislation.

q: 'Sub-delegation' of legislative power means:
o: A. The body which received delegated power further delegates to yet another body
B. The President delegates to States
C. The original legislature re-delegates to a lower body
D. Parliament delegates to the President
e: Sub-delegation occurs when a body that has received legislative power by delegation from Parliament further delegates that power to another subordinate body. The maxim 'delegatus non potest delegare' (a delegate cannot further delegate) applies — sub-delegation is valid only if expressly or impliedly permitted by the parent Act.

q: Parliamentary control over delegated legislation operates through:
o: A. Laying before Parliament — affirmative or negative resolution
e: Parliamentary control over delegated legislation operates through: (1) Laying procedure — affirmative resolution (both Houses must approve) or negative resolution (either House can annul within 30/40 days); (2) Committee on Subordinate Legislation in both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha which scrutinizes delegated legislation.

q: The doctrine of 'Legitimate Expectation' was held to give only PROCEDURAL rights (not substantive benefit) by the SC in:
o: A. Navjyoti Coop. v. Union of India
B. Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu
C. Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993)
D. M/s Javed Ahmed v. State of Maharashtra
e: In Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993), the Supreme Court held that Legitimate Expectation gives a procedural right — the right to be heard before the expectation is defeated — but NOT a substantive right to the promised benefit. The authority can still change policy for public good.

q: 'Promissory Estoppel' against the Government was confirmed in Indian law in which case?
o: A. A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India
B. M/s Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP (1979)
C. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. v. Ulhas Nagar Municipality
D. State of Punjab v. Okara Grain Buyers
e: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP (1979), the Supreme Court confirmed that the doctrine of promissory estoppel applies against the Government in India. The State had given an exemption from sales tax and the SC held the Government was estopped from withdrawing it after the company acted on the representation. Concept note: Promissory Estoppel vs Legitimate Expectation: Promissory Estoppel — equitable doctrine; government cannot retract a representation if the party acted on it to its detriment. Legitimate Expectation — public law doctrine; gives right to be heard before expectation is defeated, but not necessarily the promised benefit.

q: 'Reasoned decision' as a requirement of natural justice is NOT mandatory when:
o: A. The decision is merely recommendatory
B. The statute expressly excludes it
C. It concerns national security or confidential matters
e: Duty to give reasons can be excluded when: (1) the decision is merely recommendatory and not final; (2) the statute expressly excludes the requirement; (3) reasons would endanger national security or confidential information; (4) where the context makes it impractical.

q: Which case established that the right to cross-examine witnesses is NOT always part of natural justice in administrative proceedings?
o: B. Board of Education v. Rice (1911)
C. Russell v. Duke of Norfolk (1949)
e: In Russell v. Duke of Norfolk (1949), the court held that the requirements of natural justice depend on the circumstances of the case, the statutory framework, and the nature of inquiry. Cross-examination of witnesses is not always required — it depends on whether it would materially assist the inquiry.

q: The maxim 'Nemo bis punitur pro eodem delicto' means:
o: B. Act of the court shall not harm anyone
C. No one shall be a judge in his own cause
D. No one shall be punished twice for the same offence — relates to double jeopardy (Article 20(2))
e: Nemo bis punitur pro eodem delicto means 'no one shall be punished twice for the same offence.' It is the foundation of the double jeopardy rule in Article 20(2) of the Constitution which provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

q: In which case did the SC hold that natural justice is flexible and depends on statutory context, nature of power, and consequences for the individual?
o: A. Union of India v. Col. J.N. Sinha (1970)
B. A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1970)
C. Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India (1981)
D. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
e: In Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court held that natural justice is not a monolithic or inflexible concept. Its content and extent depend on: (1) the statutory framework; (2) the nature of the power exercised; (3) the consequences for the person affected; (4) public interest considerations.

q: Under the 'Doctrine of Fairness' in administrative law, the concept of fairness:
o: A. Is identical to natural justice
C. Is narrower than natural justice
D. Is wider than natural justice and can apply even where there is no traditional NJ requirement — based on good administration
e: The 'duty to act fairly' has emerged as a broader concept than the traditional rules of natural justice. It looks at the overall fairness of the administrative process and applies even in situations where the strict rules of natural justice may not be triggered. It evolved in English and Indian administrative law post-Maneka Gandhi.

q: 'Jurisdictional error' in administrative law traditionally referred to:
o: A. Any error of law in a decision
B. An error going to the root of jurisdiction — acting without jurisdiction, exceeding jurisdiction, or refusing to exercise jurisdiction
C. An error in applying the law correctly within jurisdiction
e: Traditional jurisdictional errors were of three types: (1) No jurisdiction — acting without any authority; (2) Excess of jurisdiction — exceeding the granted authority; (3) Failure to exercise jurisdiction — refusing to exercise power lawfully vested. Anisminic (1969) effectively widened this to include all errors of law.

q: The 'Doctrine of Proportionality' is STRICTER than Wednesbury unreasonableness in the sense that:
o: A. Proportionality gives more deference to administration
B. Proportionality applies only to criminal matters
C. Under proportionality, courts examine whether less restrictive means could be used — performing a balancing exercise; Wednesbury only asks if the decision was outrageous
D. Courts can substitute their own decision for the administrative decision
e: Wednesbury asks: was the decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it? Proportionality asks: (1) Was the objective legitimate? (2) Were the means suitable? (3) Were the means necessary — could less restrictive means achieve the same goal? (4) Was there a fair balance between rights and public interest? Proportionality is a much more intensive review.

q: 'Colourable exercise of power' in judicial review of administrative action means:
o: A. The authority made an error of fact
B. The authority acted with improper motive — exercises a power for an unauthorized purpose
C. The authority exceeded its jurisdiction
e: Colourable exercise of power (also called 'abuse of power' or 'fraud on power') means the authority exercises its power for a purpose other than the one for which it was granted — i.e., the purpose was dressed up as something else. The substance, not the form, is examined.

q: Which of the following is the CORRECT order of remedies from most available to most restricted?
o: A. Quo Warranto → Habeas Corpus → Certiorari
B. Habeas Corpus → Mandamus → Certiorari → Prohibition → Quo Warranto
C. Certiorari → Mandamus → Prohibition → Habeas Corpus → Quo Warranto
D. No particular order — all equally available
e: Habeas Corpus is the most readily available writ for protection of personal liberty — any person can apply regardless of locus standi in cases of illegal detention. Quo Warranto is the most restricted — it can only be sought against a person holding a public office without authority. The others fall in between.

q: The 'Doctrine of Exhaustion of Remedies' in judicial review means:
o: A. A party must exhaust all available statutory/alternative remedies before seeking judicial review, unless those remedies are inadequate or the case involves FRs or jurisdictional issues
B. Courts should always be approached first
C. Only applies in criminal matters
D. Writs cannot be filed at all if any other remedy exists
e: The Doctrine of Exhaustion of Remedies is a procedural doctrine — courts generally require parties to exhaust available alternative remedies before granting judicial review. Exceptions: (1) alternative remedy is inadequate/illusory; (2) Fundamental Rights are directly infringed; (3) pure jurisdictional question; (4) natural justice violation. It is a rule of prudence, not an absolute bar.

q: In Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court established that judicial review of government contracts:
o: A. Is not available for commercial decisions
B. Applies the same strict standard as constitutional review
C. Is available but courts should not substitute their commercial judgment — review limited to illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety
D. Government contracts are immune from judicial review
e: In Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994), the SC adopted Lord Diplock's three grounds from the GCHQ case for reviewing government contracts. Courts do not sit as a tender evaluation body — they only examine whether the process was legal, rational, and procedurally proper. Commercial wisdom of the decision is not reviewed.

q: The 'Doctrine of Pleasure' under Article 310 does NOT apply to:
o: A. Officers of All India Services
C. Constitutional authorities appointed under special provisions
D. Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts — they hold office 'during good behaviour'
e: Article 310 establishes the doctrine of pleasure for government servants. However, judges of the SC (Article 124) and HC (Article 217) hold office during 'good behaviour' — they can only be removed by the impeachment process under Articles 124(4) and 217(1)(b)/(3), not at the pleasure of the President.

q: Assertion (A): The Governor cannot be sued in a personal capacity during tenure. Reason (R): Article 361 confers complete immunity from criminal proceedings and civil proceedings during tenure.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
B. Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation
C. A is true but R is false
D. A is false but R is true
e: Article 361 provides complete immunity to the President and Governor: no criminal proceedings during tenure, and for civil proceedings for personal acts, 2 months' notice is required. R correctly and completely explains A.

q: Assertion (A): National Emergency once proclaimed continues indefinitely unless revoked. Reason (R): Parliamentary approval by special majority is required every six months for continuation.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
B. Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation
C. A is true but R is false
D. A is false but R is true
e: A is false because National Emergency does NOT continue indefinitely — it requires 6-monthly renewal by special majority. R is true — the mechanism is 6-monthly renewal by special majority under Article 352(6). A is the wrong statement; R is the correct rule.

q: Assertion (A): Article 200 empowers Governor to withhold assent to a Bill passed by State Legislature. Reason (R): If Governor withholds assent and State Legislature re-passes the Bill, Governor must give assent.
o: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
B. Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
C. A is true but R is false — Governor can again withhold
D. A is false but R is true
e: A is true — Article 200 does empower the Governor to withhold assent. R is also true — if the State Legislature re-passes a Bill, the Governor must give assent. But R is not the EXPLANATION of A — it is a separate rule about the consequence of re-passing. The two propositions are related but R does not explain A.

q: Match: (i) Article 123 (ii) Article 213 (iii) Article 72 (iv) Article 161 with (a) Ordinance by Governor (b) Pardoning power of President (c) Ordinance by President (d) Pardoning power of Governor
e: Article 123 (c) — President's Ordinance-making power. Article 213 (a) — Governor's Ordinance-making power. Article 72 (b) — President's pardoning power including death sentences. Article 161 (d) — Governor's pardoning power (State law offences, NOT death sentences).

q: Which of the following about Parliamentary privileges is/are CORRECT? (i) Freedom of speech in Parliament is absolute; (ii) A Member can be arrested for a criminal offence even during session; (iii) Parliamentary proceedings cannot be questioned in any court; (iv) Strangers can be excluded from galleries
e: (i) is INCORRECT — freedom of speech in Parliament is subject to rules/orders of Parliament, not absolute; (ii) CORRECT — no immunity from criminal arrest (only civil arrest immunity); (iii) CORRECT — Article 105(2) courts cannot question proceedings; (iv) CORRECT — both Houses can exclude strangers from galleries during session.

q: Arrange these Constitutional Amendments in chronological order (earliest first): (i) Insertion of Fundamental Duties (51-A); (ii) Right to Property ceased to be Fundamental Right; (iii) 'Socialist' and 'Secular' in Preamble; (iv) 10th Schedule (Anti-Defection)
e: 42nd Amendment, 1976 — inserted both (iii) 'Socialist' and 'Secular' in Preamble AND (i) Fundamental Duties (Art. 51-A) in the same amendment. 44th Amendment, 1978 — removed (ii) right to property as FR. 52nd Amendment, 1985 — inserted (iv) Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law).

q: Which of the following Schedules relates to the languages recognized by the Constitution?
e: The Eighth Schedule contains the list of languages officially recognized by the Constitution. Originally 14 languages at inception; now 22 languages after various amendments. The 8th Schedule is also relevant for Official Language purposes under Articles 344 and 351.

q: Under Article 344, the President shall constitute an Official Languages Commission within how many years of commencement of Constitution?
e: Article 344 requires the President to constitute a Commission at the expiration of 5 years from commencement of the Constitution, and again at the expiration of 10 years, to report on the progressive use of Hindi as official language and restrictions on the use of English.

q: The 'Three Lists' system of legislative distribution in the Indian Constitution was immediately borrowed from:
e: The three-list scheme (Federal List, Provincial List, Concurrent List) was first introduced in the Government of India Act, 1935. The Constitution carried this forward as Union List, State List, and Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule. Canada's Constitution had two lists; the US has enumerated + reserved powers.

q: 'Judicial activism' in India is associated with the expansion of jurisdiction through:
o: A. Limiting the scope of writ jurisdiction
B. Strict application of procedural rules
C. PIL, epistolary jurisdiction, and expanded interpretation of Article 21
D. Refusing to interfere in executive matters
e: Judicial activism in India is associated with: (1) Public Interest Litigation (PIL) — any public spirited person can approach courts; (2) Epistolary jurisdiction — letters to the court can be treated as writ petitions; (3) Expansive interpretation of Article 21 to include numerous uncontained rights. Pioneered by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer.

q: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court:
o: A. Declared sexual harassment at workplace as a criminal offence
B. Ordered Parliament to legislate within 3 months
C. Laid down guidelines treating sexual harassment at workplace as violation of Articles 14, 19, and 21 — filled the legislative vacuum
D. Upheld conviction under existing law
e: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) — the SC laid down the Vishaka Guidelines treating sexual harassment at workplace as a violation of Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g), and 21. These Guidelines had the force of law until the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 was enacted.

q: The Punchhi Commission (2010) was set up to review:
o: B. Centre-State relations broadly — constitutional federalism, Governor's role, Article 356, inter-State water disputes
e: The Punchhi Commission (headed by former CJI Madan Mohan Punchhi, 2010) was constituted to review the working of the constitutional scheme of Centre-State relations. It recommended: restraint in use of Art. 356; Governors to be constitutional heads; delimitation of Governor's discretionary powers; strengthening Inter-State Council.

q: Which Article provides for an independent body to audit accounts of the Union and States — the CAG?
o: A. Article 148 — Comptroller and Auditor General of India
e: Article 148 establishes the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. The CAG is appointed by the President and can be removed only in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge. Article 149 defines the duties and powers of CAG. Article 151 provides for presentation of CAG reports to Parliament/State Legislature.

q: After the 44th Amendment, 1978, which two Fundamental Rights CANNOT be suspended even during National Emergency?
e: The 44th Amendment, 1978 amended Article 359 to provide that the President cannot suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 even during a National Emergency. This was a direct response to the abuse of emergency powers during 1975-77.

q: In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh (2016), the Supreme Court held:
o: A. The Speaker can be removed by the Governor
B. The Governor has absolute discretion in all Assembly matters
C. The Governor's power to advance the session was unconstitutional — he cannot act contrary to advice of Council of Ministers on summoning sessions
D. The Governor can summon a session of the Assembly at any time on his own
e: In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016), the SC held that summoning, proroguing, and dissolving the State Legislative Assembly are matters on which the Governor must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Governor cannot advance the session on his own to destabilize an elected government.

q: In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the nine-judge bench held regarding the Ninth Schedule:
o: A. All laws in the Ninth Schedule are immune from all Constitutional challenges
B. The Ninth Schedule is itself unconstitutional
C. Only property-related laws in Ninth Schedule are protected
D. Laws before April 24, 1973 are fully protected; laws after that date can be challenged if they violate basic structure or damage FRs forming part of basic structure
e: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) — 9-judge bench held: laws inserted in 9th Schedule before April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda Bharati) are fully protected; laws inserted after that date are open to challenge if they violate the basic structure or if fundamental rights forming part of basic structure are abrogated.

q: Article 32(4) provides that the right under Article 32 shall NOT be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution. This means:
o: A. Art. 32 can be suspended by the Supreme Court
B. Art. 32 can be suspended only under Art. 359 (National Emergency Presidential Order) — and even then only if Arts. 20 & 21 are not involved
C. Art. 32 can be suspended by Parliament anytime
D. Art. 32 cannot be suspended under any circumstances whatsoever
e: Article 32(4) provides that the right under Article 32 cannot be suspended except as otherwise provided by the Constitution. The only provision that allows suspension is Article 359 (Presidential Order during National Emergency). But even then, Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended, so the right to enforce them under Art. 32 remains.

q: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court's 7-judge bench overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) and held:
o: A. MPs who take bribes to vote have NO immunity under Article 105 — bribery is not protected by parliamentary privilege
B. MPs who take bribes to vote are protected under Article 105(2)
C. Members of State Legislatures are also protected from bribery charges
D. All parliamentary activities are absolutely protected
e: Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024) — a 7-judge constitutional bench unanimously overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) and held that the immunity under Article 105(2) does not extend to bribery. A Member of Parliament who takes a bribe to vote in a particular manner cannot claim the protection of parliamentary privilege.
